listeningParts.title: Booking a school visit to a space centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A teacher phones a space science centre to book a visit for her class.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Good morning, Northgate Space Centre, bookings desk. This is Oliver speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Hi, good morning. I'm a teacher at a primary school, and I'd like to book a visit for my class next term. We're studying the solar system, and I've heard your centre is excellent for children.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you, that's lovely to hear. I can certainly help with that. How many children would be coming?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: There are thirty-two in the class, but two of them will be away on that week, so it'll be thirty pupils.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thirty pupils. And how old are they?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: They're nine and ten years old.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Perfect. For that age group, we recommend our Explorer Day. It includes a show in the planetarium, a guided tour of the main galleries and one workshop. Did you have a date in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: We were hoping for a Thursday in May. Would the fifteenth be possible?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm afraid the fifteenth is already fully booked, but we have space on Thursday the twenty-second.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: The twenty-second would be fine. That's still before the half-term holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Great. Now, for the workshop, there are three choices. The first is Rocket Science, where the children build and launch small rockets powered by water and air. The second is Life on the Space Station, where they find out how astronauts eat, sleep and exercise. And the third is Mission to Mars, where they work in teams to design a vehicle that could drive on the surface of Mars.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Hmm. They'd all love the rockets, but I think the Mars one fits best with our topic, because we're going to look at the planets in detail.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Mission to Mars it is, then. It's very popular, and the children get to test their designs on our model Martian landscape at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Wonderful. What time does the day start?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: We ask groups to arrive by half past nine. The planetarium show begins at a quarter to ten, and the day finishes at half past two, so that you can get back to school before the end of the day.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: That works. And what about lunch? We'll bring packed lunches.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: That's what most schools do. We have a lunch room for school groups on the ground floor, next to the shop. You'll have it from twelve until half past twelve. You can also leave bags and coats there during the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Good. And how much does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: The Explorer Day is eight pounds fifty per child. Adults are free, as long as there's at least one adult for every ten children. Any extra adults pay six pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: So with thirty children, we need three adults. I'll probably bring four, with myself and three parents. Is that a problem?

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Not at all. The fourth adult would just pay the six pounds. Now, can I take some details? What's the name of your school?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: It's Hollybank Primary School.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: And your name?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Mrs Karen Lindqvist. That's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Thank you. Will you be coming by coach?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Yes, we will.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: Then please tell the driver to use the entrance on Mill Lane, not the main entrance, because coaches can drop off and park there. And one more thing: please let us know at least a week before your visit if any children need extra support, or use a wheelchair, so that we can make sure everything is ready.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: One of the boys does use a wheelchair, actually.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.text: That's no problem at all. The whole building is accessible, and I'll make a note on the booking. We'll send you a confirmation by email, along with a worksheet that the children can complete during the gallery tour.

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Lovely. Thanks so much for your help.

listeningParts.title: A summer space camp
listeningParts.contextDescription: The organiser of a week-long summer space camp for teenagers speaks to parents at an information evening.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name is Rachel Torres, and I'm the director of Orbit Space Camp. Tonight I'd like to tell you what your children will be doing during the week, and answer some of the questions that parents usually ask.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: First, a bit about us. Orbit Space Camp started eleven years ago, with just twenty students in a borrowed school hall. Today we welcome around two hundred young people every summer, aged between twelve and sixteen, and we're based here at the university, which means we can use the science labs, the sports hall and the observatory on the roof. Most of our staff are science teachers or university students studying physics or engineering, and every group of eight campers has its own team leader.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Now, the programme. The week is built around a single big challenge: each team has to plan and carry out an imaginary mission to the Moon. Everything they do during the week helps them prepare for that.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: On Monday, after the welcome session, the teams are formed and each one chooses a name and designs a mission badge. In the afternoon, there's a talk about the history of space travel, and we're very lucky this year, because the talk will be given by a retired engineer who worked on satellite design for over thirty years.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: On Tuesday, the focus is on rockets. Campers learn the basic science of how rockets work, and then they build their own model rockets, which are launched on the sports field. It's always one of the favourite days, although it can get a little muddy if it rains, so please pack an old pair of shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Wednesday is all about living in space. The campers try some of the food that astronauts eat, which, I should warn you, not all of them enjoy. They also find out how astronauts keep fit, and they try our simulator, which gives them an idea of how difficult it is to move around without gravity.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: On Thursday, the teams finish planning their missions, and in the evening, if the sky is clear, we hold our stargazing session at the observatory. That means a late finish, at about eleven o'clock, so you'll need to collect your children later that day, or they can stay overnight in the university accommodation for a small extra charge. If it's cloudy, we'll show a film in the lecture theatre instead.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And finally, on Friday, the teams carry out their missions. One room becomes mission control, and the teams have to deal with unexpected problems that we give them, just like real flight controllers. In the afternoon, parents are invited to a presentation, where each team explains its mission, and everyone receives a certificate.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical matters. The camp runs from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon, apart from Thursday. Lunch is provided every day in the university canteen, and we can cater for all special diets, as long as you tell us on the registration form. Please don't send your children with large amounts of money; there's nothing to buy apart from snacks and a small shop that sells camp T-shirts.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Mobile phones are allowed, but they must be switched off during activities. We find that the campers are usually far too busy to miss them. And if you need to contact your child during the day, please call the camp office rather than their mobile.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Finally, a question I'm always asked: do children need to be good at science? The answer is no. Many of our campers simply have an interest in space, and some of our most creative mission plans have come from students who say they don't like science at school. Right, I'm happy to take your questions now.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on the Voyager missions
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two astronomy students, Lena and Sam, discuss their presentation on the Voyager space probes with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Lena, Sam. So you've chosen the Voyager missions for your presentation. Tell me how you're planning to organise it.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Well, we want to start with the background, explaining why the two probes were launched when they were. Then we'll look at what they discovered at the planets, and finish with where they are now.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds logical. So why were they launched in 1977?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Because of a rare arrangement of the outer planets. In the late nineteen-seventies, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune were lined up in a way that only happens about once every hundred and seventy-five years. That meant a spacecraft could use the gravity of one planet to speed it up and bend its path towards the next one. It's called a gravity assist.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And without that, the journey would have taken far longer?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Much longer, decades longer for Neptune. One thing that confuses people is that Voyager 2 was actually launched first, in August 1977, and Voyager 1 about two weeks later, in September. But Voyager 1 was on a faster route, so it overtook its twin and reached Jupiter first.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: We thought we'd use a timeline to show that, because it's easier to follow than just saying the dates.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good idea. Now, the discoveries. There's a huge amount you could say, so you'll have to be selective.

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: We know. We've decided to choose one discovery for each planet. For Jupiter, it's the volcanoes on its moon Io. Nobody expected to find active volcanoes anywhere except Earth, so that was a real surprise. For Saturn, we're going to talk about the structure of the rings, which turned out to be made of thousands of narrow rings rather than a few wide ones.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And then for Uranus and Neptune, it's important to say that Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft that has ever visited them. It flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. At Neptune, it found a huge storm, which was called the Great Dark Spot.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. And will you mention the Golden Record?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Definitely. Both probes carry a gold-plated record with sounds and images from Earth, including greetings in fifty-five languages and different kinds of music. The committee that chose the contents was led by the astronomer Carl Sagan. We'd like to play a short clip from it during the presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That'll certainly keep the audience's attention. Just check that the clip isn't too long; you only have fifteen minutes in total.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: We'll keep it under thirty seconds. Then, for the last part, we want to talk about the famous photograph called the Pale Blue Dot, which Voyager 1 took in 1990, looking back at Earth from about six billion kilometres away. Earth is just a tiny point of light in it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a powerful image to show. And where are the probes now?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: Both of them have left the bubble of particles from the Sun and entered interstellar space: Voyager 1 in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018. They're the most distant human-made objects ever. Radio signals from Voyager 1 now take nearly a day to reach Earth.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The problem is power. They run on a nuclear power source that produces a little less electricity every year, so the engineers have been switching off instruments one by one to save energy. At some point in the next few years, they won't have enough power to send signals at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what do you think the main message of your presentation is?

dialogue.speaker: Lena
dialogue.text: I suppose that a mission planned to last about five years has been working for nearly half a century, and that's partly thanks to the engineers, who've solved problems from billions of kilometres away.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good way to end. One piece of advice: for the slides, use fewer words and bigger pictures. The images from Voyager are so striking that they'll do a lot of the work for you.

listeningParts.title: The human body in space
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a human physiology course on how long periods in space affect astronauts' bodies.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at what happens to the human body when it spends a long time in space. This isn't just an interesting question. If people are ever going to travel to Mars, a journey that would take several months in each direction, we need to understand these effects and find ways to reduce them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Most of what we know comes from astronauts who have lived on space stations in orbit around the Earth, especially the International Space Station, where crews usually stay for about six months. The longest single stay in space was by the Russian doctor Valeri Polyakov, who spent four hundred and thirty-seven days on the Mir space station in the mid nineteen-nineties.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with the most obvious difference: the lack of gravity, or more accurately, microgravity. On Earth, our bones and muscles are constantly working against gravity, even when we're just standing still. In space, they no longer have to do this, and the body responds by losing what it doesn't need. Astronauts can lose around one to one and a half per cent of the mass of their weight-bearing bones, such as the hips and legs, every month. That's similar to the amount an elderly person on Earth might lose in a whole year. Muscles also become weaker, particularly in the legs and back.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: To reduce these effects, astronauts on the space station exercise for about two hours every day. They use a treadmill, with straps that hold them down so they don't float away, an exercise bike, and a machine that allows them to lift weights by using pressure instead of heavy objects. This has made a big difference, although it doesn't completely prevent bone loss.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A second effect concerns the body's fluids. On Earth, gravity pulls blood and other fluids down towards our feet. In space, these fluids move up towards the head. As a result, astronauts' faces look puffy and their legs become thinner, which some astronauts jokingly call 'bird legs'. This movement of fluid may also be connected to changes in vision. Some astronauts find that their eyesight becomes worse during long missions, because of changes to the shape of the eye, and in some cases the changes last after they return.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, astronauts also grow taller in space, by up to about five centimetres, because the spine is no longer being pressed together by gravity. Unfortunately, this often causes back pain, and they return to their normal height soon after landing.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Many astronauts also suffer from space sickness during their first few days, because the balance system in the inner ear becomes confused. And sleep can be difficult. Because the space station travels around the Earth about every ninety minutes, astronauts see around sixteen sunrises a day, which can disturb the body's natural daily rhythms. They usually sleep in small cabins, in sleeping bags attached to the wall.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A more serious long-term concern is radiation. On Earth, and even on the space station, we're partly protected by the Earth's magnetic field. On a journey to Mars, astronauts would be outside this protection for much longer, and exposed to higher levels of radiation, which could increase the risk of cancer. Designing better shielding for spacecraft is one of the main challenges for future missions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Finally, an unusual experiment. In 2015, the American astronaut Scott Kelly spent almost a year on the space station, while his identical twin brother, Mark, who is also a former astronaut, stayed on Earth. Because they have the same genes, scientists could compare the two men to see how spaceflight had changed Scott's body. They found a number of changes, for example in his immune system and in the way some of his genes were working, but most of them returned to normal within a few months of his return. That's encouraging news for those planning longer missions. Next week, we'll look at the psychological effects of living in a small space, far from home.

readingPassages.title: One giant leap: the road to the Moon
paragraphs: On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite. It was a metal ball about the size of a beach ball, and all it did was send out a simple radio signal as it circled the Earth. Yet its effect in the United States was enormous. Many Americans were shocked that their great rival had beaten them into space, and they feared that the same rockets could be used to carry nuclear weapons. The event marked the beginning of what became known as the Space Race.

The Soviet Union continued to lead for several years. On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, completing a single orbit of the Earth in a flight that lasted 108 minutes. Less than a month later, Alan Shepard became the first American in space, but his flight lasted only about fifteen minutes and did not go into orbit. The United States needed a goal that would be so ambitious that neither country would have an advantage at the start.

That goal was announced by President John F. Kennedy on 25 May 1961. Speaking to Congress, he said that the nation should commit itself to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth before the end of the decade. At the time, the United States had a total of just fifteen minutes of experience of human spaceflight, and many of the technologies that would be needed had not yet been invented. Over the following years, the space agency NASA grew rapidly, and in the mid-1960s its budget reached more than four per cent of all federal government spending.

Getting to the Moon required a series of steps. In the Gemini programme of 1965 and 1966, two-person crews practised the skills that would be needed later, such as spending up to two weeks in space, working outside the spacecraft and joining two spacecraft together in orbit. Meanwhile, engineers developed the Saturn V, a rocket around 110 metres tall that remains one of the most powerful ever flown. The programme also suffered a terrible setback. In January 1967, during a test on the launch pad, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 spacecraft, and its three astronauts were killed. The design of the spacecraft was changed significantly as a result.

In December 1968, the Apollo 8 mission carried three astronauts around the Moon for the first time. As they came out from behind the Moon, they saw the Earth rising above its grey horizon, and one of them, Bill Anders, took a photograph that became known as Earthrise. The picture of a small, colourful planet surrounded by the darkness of space was later credited with helping to inspire the environmental movement.

Apollo 11 was launched on 16 July 1969, carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. Four days later, while Collins remained in orbit, Armstrong and Aldrin landed the lunar module, called Eagle, on a flat area known as the Sea of Tranquility. The landing was more dangerous than many people realised. The computer was giving alarms, and the planned landing area was full of large rocks, so Armstrong took manual control and flew on to find a safer place. When the module touched down, there was very little fuel left.

Some hours later, Armstrong climbed down the ladder and stepped onto the surface, saying the famous words, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' Hundreds of millions of people around the world watched the black-and-white television pictures. The two astronauts spent about two and a half hours walking outside, setting up scientific experiments, planting a flag and collecting samples of rock and soil, before returning to orbit and travelling back to Earth. They landed safely in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July.

There were five more successful landings, and in total twelve men walked on the Moon. The last, Apollo 17, took place in December 1972. The rocks they brought back, weighing almost 400 kilograms in total, are still being studied today and have helped scientists to understand how the Moon was formed. Since then, no human has travelled further than a few hundred kilometres from the Earth. Several countries now have plans to send people back to the Moon, more than half a century after the last footprints were left there.

readingPassages.title: Robots on the red planet
paragraphs: Mars is the most explored planet in the solar system apart from our own, yet no human has ever set foot on it. Everything we know about its surface has been learned by robots. Over the past six decades, more than a dozen spacecraft have successfully orbited or landed on Mars, and their story is one of remarkable engineering, painful failures and some unexpectedly long lives.

The first successful mission was NASA's Mariner 4, which flew past Mars in July 1965 and sent back around twenty images. Before then, some people had imagined that Mars might have canals or forests. The photographs showed instead a dry surface covered in craters, more like the Moon than the Earth. In 1976, two American Viking landers became the first spacecraft to operate successfully on the surface for a long period, sending back the first colour pictures and measuring the weather for several years.

Landing on Mars is extremely difficult, and many missions have failed during the final minutes. The planet's atmosphere is thick enough to heat a spacecraft dangerously as it enters, but too thin, at less than one per cent of the pressure on Earth, to slow it down using parachutes alone. Engineers have tried several solutions. In 1997, the Mars Pathfinder mission bounced onto the surface surrounded by giant airbags, and released a small rover called Sojourner, about the size of a microwave oven, which explored the area around the landing site for nearly three months.

In January 2004, two much larger rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, landed on opposite sides of the planet. They were designed to work for about ninety Martian days, but both lasted far longer. Engineers had worried that dust would cover their solar panels and reduce their power, but from time to time, gusts of wind cleaned the panels, giving the rovers new energy. Spirit became stuck in soft ground in 2009 and stopped communicating the following year, while Opportunity kept going until a huge dust storm in 2018. By then, it had travelled more than 45 kilometres, further than a marathon.

Driving a rover on Mars is very different from steering a remote-controlled car. Depending on where the two planets are in their orbits, a radio signal takes between about three and twenty-two minutes to travel from Earth to Mars. A driver cannot react quickly to a rock or a hole in the ground. Instead, teams on Earth plan each day's activities in advance and send a set of instructions, and modern rovers use cameras and software to find a safe route by themselves. Because a Martian day is about forty minutes longer than an Earth day, team members have sometimes lived on 'Mars time', starting work later every day.

The next generation of rovers was much heavier. Curiosity, which landed in August 2012, is about the size of a small car and weighs almost a tonne, too much for airbags. It was lowered to the ground on cables from a hovering platform powered by rockets, a method called the sky crane. Instead of solar panels, Curiosity uses a nuclear power source, which allows it to work through dust storms and the Martian winter. Its instruments have shown that its landing site, Gale Crater, once contained a lake.

In February 2021, Perseverance used the same landing method to reach Jezero Crater, the site of another ancient lake. Its main task is to collect samples of rock and store them in sealed tubes, which a future mission may bring back to Earth for detailed study. Perseverance also carried a small helicopter called Ingenuity. In April 2021, it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It had been expected to make no more than five flights, but it eventually completed seventy-two before damage to its blades ended the mission in 2024.

Mars exploration is no longer limited to the United States. In 2021, China's Zhurong rover landed successfully, making China only the second country to operate a rover on the planet. Several space agencies now hope to send astronauts to Mars in the coming decades. If they succeed, the first human visitors will owe a great deal to the robots that went before them, which have mapped the ground, studied the weather and tested the technology that people will one day depend on.

readingPassages.title: Holidays beyond the sky
paragraphs: For most of the history of spaceflight, going into space was something only governments could arrange. Astronauts were highly trained pilots, scientists or engineers, chosen from thousands of applicants and paid by the state. Today, that is changing. Private companies are now selling seats on rockets to anyone who can afford them, and space tourism, once a subject for science fiction, has become a real, if very expensive, industry. Whether it deserves our enthusiasm is another matter.

The idea of ordinary people travelling into space is not new. The Russian schoolteacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, who worked out many of the basic principles of rocket science in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, famously wrote that the Earth is the cradle of humanity, but that one cannot live in the cradle forever. For him, leaving the planet was a natural step in human development rather than an adventure for a few wealthy individuals.

The first paying space tourist was the American businessman Dennis Tito, who in 2001 travelled to the International Space Station on a Russian Soyuz spacecraft. He reportedly paid around twenty million dollars for the trip, which lasted about a week. Some officials at NASA were unhappy about his visit, arguing that the space station was a place for serious work rather than sightseeing. A small number of other wealthy individuals followed him over the next few years. Each of them had to spend months training in Russia before the flight, learning how to live and work safely in a cramped spacecraft and how to respond in an emergency.

The real turning point came in July 2021, when two billionaires flew on rockets built by their own companies within nine days of each other. On 11 July, Richard Branson flew with Virgin Galactic to a height of about 86 kilometres, aboard a spaceplane launched from beneath a large aircraft. Nine days later, Jeff Bezos travelled with Blue Origin on a short flight that passed 100 kilometres, the boundary of space that is accepted by most international organisations. His crew included Wally Funk, who had trained for spaceflight in the early 1960s but had never been allowed to fly. At 82, she became, for a short time, the oldest person ever to go into space.

Experiences like these can be powerful. The writer Frank White used the term 'the overview effect' to describe the change in thinking that many astronauts report after seeing the Earth from space, often a deep sense of the planet's fragility and of the unity of humankind. Not every reaction is joyful. When the actor William Shatner flew with Blue Origin in October 2021, at the age of ninety, he later wrote that, instead of excitement, he had felt an overwhelming sadness at the contrast between the cold darkness of space and the warm, living Earth below.

Supporters of space tourism argue that it brings real benefits. The money paid by wealthy customers, they say, helps companies to develop reusable rockets and other technology, which will eventually make spaceflight cheaper for everyone, including scientists. I find this argument partly convincing. The cost of launching satellites has already fallen considerably as private companies have entered the market, and there is no reason why tourism could not contribute to the same process. It is also worth remembering that many technologies first developed for space, from improved weather forecasting to satellite navigation, are now part of everyday life on Earth, and a larger, more competitive industry may speed up such developments.

There are, however, serious concerns. With tickets on suborbital flights costing hundreds of thousands of dollars, space tourism is currently available only to a tiny number of very rich people. Some atmospheric scientists have also warned that rockets release soot directly into the upper atmosphere, where it may remain far longer than pollution released near the ground. In my view, these environmental questions have not received nearly enough attention, and they should be studied carefully before the number of flights increases.

Will space tourism ever become an ordinary holiday? It seems unlikely in the near future. But aviation also began as a dangerous and expensive activity for a privileged few, and within a few decades millions of people were flying every year. What matters, I would argue, is not whether the first space tourists are rich, but whether the industry is properly regulated, so that the benefits of new technology are widely shared and the costs to the planet are not ignored. If that happens, Tsiolkovsky's dream may yet come true.
